topic: A new dress code at work
context: The company you work for has decided to introduce a formal dress code. The director has written to all staff.

paragraphs: From next month all staff will be expected to wear formal business dress in the office, including on days when no clients are visiting.
The aim is to present a consistent professional image. We understand that this is a significant change and we would welcome your views before the rule takes effect.

task11: Write a message to a colleague who is a close friend. Write about your feelings about the new rule and what you intend to do.
task12: Write an email to the director. Give your views on the new dress code and suggest how the rule could be made to work better for staff.
part2_question: Does what people wear at work affect how well they do their job?

task11: Have you read the director's email about formal dress every day? I think it is unnecessary, since most of us never see a client. I am not going to ignore it, but I will write and suggest keeping Fridays casual. Are you going to reply as well?
task12: Thank you for inviting our views before the new dress code begins. I understand the wish for a consistent professional image, and I have no objection to formal dress when clients are in the building.

I would question the need for it every day, however. My team works almost entirely by telephone and email, and the rule would mean a considerable expense for colleagues who do not own several suits. Several of them have mentioned the cost to me privately but would not raise it with you directly.

Might I suggest a compromise? Formal dress on client days and on Mondays, smart casual otherwise, with the standard defined clearly so that nobody is left guessing. A small allowance towards the first purchase would also be welcomed by younger staff.
part2: Whether clothing affects performance at work is a question people answer very differently, and the honest reply is that it matters, but much less than employers believe.

There is something in the argument for formality. Dressing deliberately marks the start of the working day, which helps concentration, and in jobs built on trust — law, medicine, banking — a client reads appearance as evidence of competence before a word is spoken.

Against that stands the experience of the last few years. Millions of people worked from home in whatever they liked and output did not collapse; in many firms it rose. What actually drives performance is clear objectives, a manageable workload and a manager worth working for, none of which has anything to do with a tie. Uniforms in schools make the same point: they signal a shared purpose more than they improve any individual's work.

My own view is that a dress code is worth having where clients see the work, and is otherwise a distraction from the things that genuinely determine how well a job is done. A rule that nobody can explain is simply resented, and resentment costs an employer far more than an open collar.
